title: settlement.processed always throws ReferenceError: `body` is not in scope, so fundsReceivedAt is never set and no vendor payout ever becomes eligible
evidence: processWebhookEvent's signature (line 207-213) is `async ({ record, event, ids, account, isReplay = false }) => {` — there is no `body`. Line 259 inside it: `return handleGatewaySettlement({ body, account, finish });`. `handleGatewaySettlement` (line 425) is a nested declaration inside processWebhookEvent, so the only other `body` in the file is `handleRazorpayWebhook`'s own parameter (line 821) — a sibling scope, not an enclosing one. `grep -n body` over the file confirms no module-level or enclosing binding. Verified at runtime: evaluating the identifier inside a function with that exact parameter list yields `ReferenceError: body is not defined`.
failure_scenario: Razorpay delivers `settlement.processed` (it is in WEBHOOK_HANDLED_EVENTS, constants/webhook.js:101). processWebhookEvent reaches line 259 and throws ReferenceError before `handleGatewaySettlement` is entered. handleRazorpayWebhook's catch (line 917) marks the delivery FAILED and pages admins, and answers 200 so Razorpay never retries. `recordFundsReceived` is therefore never called — grep shows helpers/transactions/recordFundsReceived.js has exactly one non-test caller, this dead branch (line 468). Settlement eligibility requires `fundsReceivedAt: { $ne: null, ... }` (helpers/settlements/settlementClaims.js:88), so no transaction ever becomes eligible and no vendor is ever paid. Replay does not help: replayWebhookEvent.js:100 calls the same processWebhookEvent and hits the same line (it also omits `account`).
suggested_fix: Add `body` to processWebhookEvent's parameter list and pass `body: record.payload` from both call sites (handleRazorpayWebhook line 916 and replayWebhookEvent line 100 — the latter must also pass `account: record.account`), or read the settlement entity from `record.payload` inside handleGatewaySettlement instead of from a `body` argument.

title: ABANDONED is unreachable, so a FAILED settlement whose brand has no verified bank strands its rows for ever
evidence:
constants/settlement.js:106-110 — [SETTLEMENT_STATUS.FAILED]: Object.freeze([SETTLEMENT_STATUS.APPROVED, SETTLEMENT_STATUS.ABANDONED]).
constants/settlement.js:49-50 — ABANDONED: "A FAILED settlement nobody will retry. The only way FAILED releases."
constants/settlement.js:154-164 — SETTLEMENT_RELEASING_STATUSES includes ABANDONED.
But nothing ever writes it: `grep -rn "ABANDONED" services/ controllers/ routes/ helpers/ validator/ jobs/` returns only two comment/label hits (settlementJobs.js:329, buildSettlementReadPipeline.js:194). There is no /abandon route in routes/settlements.js and no `to: SETTLEMENT_STATUS.ABANDONED` call anywhere.
The only other FAILED exit is retryPayout, which refuses without a live verified bank — paySettlement.js:341-347: `const fresh = await liveBankSnapshot(settlement.brandId); if (!fresh) throwError(422, "This brand still has no verified bank account...")`.
cancelSettlement is also barred: ALLOWED[FAILED] does not contain CANCELLED, so transitionSettlement.js:67-79 throws 422.
failure_scenario: Brand B's NEFT bounces (failPayout -> FAILED, rows deliberately NOT released). B then closes the account / the Bank row is soft-deleted or its isVerified goes false (liveBankSnapshot returns null at paySettlement.js:429). Admin clicks retry -> 422 forever. Admin clicks cancel -> 422 "A failed settlement cannot become cancelled. It can only go to: approved, abandoned" — and there is no way to reach abandoned. The settlement's Transactions keep settlementId = S, so buildEligibilityFilter's `settlementId: null` (settlementClaims.js:57) never matches them again. Every rupee in that cycle is invisible to every future build, permanently, with no error and no log. alertLateSettlements fires once (overdueAlertsSent: { $lt: 1 }, settlementJobs.js:157) and then goes quiet.
suggested_fix: Add an admin abandon endpoint that calls transitionSettlement({ to: ABANDONED }) — it already releases via SETTLEMENT_RELEASING_STATUSES. Until then FAILED has no reachable releasing exit. Also consider adding CANCELLED to ALLOWED[FAILED] so an admin has a second door.

title: startPayout never checks needsRevalidation, so a taint that lands after approval is paid out anyway
evidence:
startPayout's only guards are paySettlement.js:73 `if (settlement.status !== SETTLEMENT_STATUS.APPROVED)`, :80 `if (!(settlement.netPayable > 0))` and :90 `await assertBankUnchanged(...)`. `needsRevalidation` appears nowhere in paySettlement.js except line 354 where retryPayout *clears* it.
taintSettlement.js:49-61 deliberately accepts APPROVED: `status: { $in: SETTLEMENT_PRE_PAYOUT_STATUSES }`, and constants/settlement.js:183-187 defines that as [DRAFT, PENDING_APPROVAL, APPROVED] with the comment "A risk event landing on a transaction in one of these can still be excluded for free."
The only enforcement of the flag is inside approveSettlement.js:88-93 (`needsRevalidation: { $ne: true }` in the update filter), which has already run by then.
failure_scenario: 02:00 build claims txn T into settlement S. 10:00 admin approves S (flag clear, approval succeeds). 11:00 Razorpay sends dispute.created on T, or a customer files a refund — taintSettlement stamps needsRevalidation: true + taintedTransactionIds: [T] on S because APPROVED is in the pre-payout list, and handleRazorpayWebhook.js:733-746 emails the admin "rebuild it before approving". The admin's next click is not approve, it is PATCH /admin/:id/pay, which reads none of that: the leg is created for the full netPayable and the NEFT goes out including T's money, which is simultaneously being charged back / refunded to the customer. NEFT has no recall.
suggested_fix: Put `needsRevalidation: { $ne: true }` in a conditional claim in startPayout (or refuse with the describeTaintedRows message and park ON_HOLD), the same way approveSettlement does. A read-then-write `if` is not enough — the flag can land between the read and the leg creation.

title: A resolved chargeback leaves settlementHold on for ever — no code path anywhere can clear it
evidence:
handleRazorpayWebhook.js:686-704 — every dispute event, resolved or not, writes:
  isDisputed: isOpen,            // false for WON / LOST / CLOSED (line 677-687)
  settlementHold: true,
  settlementHoldReason: `Chargeback ${disputeStatus} (${dispute.id})`,
with the comment at :699-701 "A webhook never takes it off: releasing it is an explicit admin action."

That admin action does not exist. A full-repo grep for writes of settlementHold finds exactly one place that sets it false — helpers/refunds/releaseSettlementHold.js:78 — and it has exactly three callers, all refund terminal states: services/refunds/decideRefund.js:192 (VENDOR_REJECTED), decideRefund.js:264 (CANCELLED), services/refunds/executeRefund.js:161 (ADMIN_REJECTED). No controller, route or validator mentions settlementHold (grep over controllers/ and routes/ returns nothing; routes/settlements.js:74 `/admin/:settlementId/hold` is Settlement.status, a different field). No job touches it either — services/refunds/refundJobs.js:167-195 only ever sets it true.
failure_scenario: A ₹810 voucher claim is charged back. `payment.dispute.created` → settlementHold: true. We submit evidence and win: `payment.dispute.won` lands 45 days later and writes isDisputed: false, disputeResolvedAt: now, settlementHold: true (again). The transaction now has settlementHold: true, isDisputed: false, amountRefunded: 0, settlementId: null, no RefundRequest at all. helpers/settlements/settlementClaims.js:66 requires `settlementHold: false`, so this payment is skipped by every settlement cycle from now until the end of time. Nothing errors, nothing logs, no health counter moves (see the separate finding on getPaymentHealth). The vendor's money for that sale is frozen permanently and the only recovery is a hand-written Mongo update.
suggested_fix: Add the admin release the webhook comment promises: a `releaseHoldAfterDispute` service + admin endpoint that clears settlementHold on a transaction whose disputeResolvedAt is set and disputeStatus is WON/CLOSED, records who released it and why in settlementHoldReleaseReason, and refuses on disputeStatus LOST. Until it exists, the dispute branch is writing a field that has no exit.

title: releaseSettlementHold clears a hold placed by a LOST chargeback, because its dispute guard passes once the dispute resolves
failure_scenario: Customer both files a refund request and charges back with their bank (routine). Sequence: refund REQUESTED → hold on. `payment.dispute.created` → hold on, isDisputed true. 60 days later `payment.dispute.lost` → the issuer debits us ₹810; isDisputed: false, disputeResolvedAt set, hold still on. The refund request has been sitting in the admin worklist all this time (getPaymentHealth.js:197 `unattendedEscalations` counts exactly these), and an admin now closes it — rejectRefundAsAdmin (executeRefund.js:161) or the customer withdraws it (decideRefund.js:264). releaseSettlementHold sees isDisputed false, no other open refund, and sets settlementHold: false with reason "Refund declined after review". The row is now fully eligible; the next buildSettlements claims it and pays the vendor the full netBill for money the issuing bank has already taken back from us. Straight loss, and the settlement statement is internally consistent so nothing flags it.
suggested_fix: Make the release conditional on the hold being this refund's. Either add a `settlementHoldSource` field and put it in the updateOne filter (`{ _id, settlementHoldSource: 'REFUND' }`), or block on the dispute record rather than on liveness: refuse while `disputeStatus` is LOST at all, and while `disputeId` is set without an explicit admin release. Making the write conditional also closes the read-then-write race — a dispute webhook landing between the .lean() read at :47 and the updateOne at :74 currently has its brand-new hold silently wiped.

title: Refund double-credits the vendor's promo share — VENDOR_PAYABLE never returns to zero on a full refund
failure_scenario:
Live today (promo codes are shipped; postCaptureEntries.js:17-24 uses this exact example). Claim: bill 1000, 20% offer -> netBill 800; promo 50 split 30/70 -> vendorPromoCost 15, platformPromoCost 35; fee 10; commission 0. Customer pays 760.
Capture rows: COLLECTION +800, VENDOR_PROMO_SHARE -15 -> getVendorBalance = 785 (asserted in __tests__/money/ledger.test.js:311).
Customer is then refunded the full 760. calculateRefundSplit returns vendorClawback 785, vendorPromoReversal 15 (verified by running the helper).
Refund rows: COLLECTION -785, VENDOR_PROMO_SHARE +15.
Balance after a FULL refund = 785 - 785 + 15 = +15.00, not 0.
The ledger now says we still owe this brand Rs.15 for a sale that was entirely reversed, and it says so silently — there is no reconcileLedger job in the repo (grep for reconcileLedger finds only comments), so nothing ever reports the drift. Every promo-funded claim that is refunded leaves its own permanent residue; the error accumulates monotonically and is real money once anything pays out against getVendorBalance. The refund tests never catch it because __tests__/money/refundCompletion.test.js:52 sets vendorPromoCost: 0.
suggested_fix: The COLLECTION refund row must mirror the COLLECTION capture row, so it must carry split.netBillRefund (the gross reversal), not split.vendorClawback. With COLLECTION -netBillRefund and VENDOR_PROMO_SHARE +vendorPromoReversal the vendor side nets to exactly -(netBillRefund - vendorPromoReversal) and a full refund returns the balance to zero. Add a regression test with a non-zero vendorPromoCost asserting getVendorBalance === 0 after a full refund.

title: reconcileRefunds re-applies settlementHold but never taints the settlement, so the job that exists to stop paying a vendor for a claim under refund does not stop it
failure_scenario: requestRefund creates the RefundRequest (refundRequest.js:184) and the process dies before line 228 — exactly the crash the job's own docstring (refundJobs.js:157-163) names. The next hourly buildSettlements sees settlementHold still false, claims the transaction into a DRAFT and moves it to PENDING_APPROVAL (buildSettlements.js:172-213). reconcileRefunds then runs repairMissingHolds: settlementHold becomes true, but the settlement keeps needsRevalidation:false and an empty taintedTransactionIds. An admin approves (approveSettlement.js:92 matches), the MANUAL_BANK NEFT goes out, and the vendor is paid in full for a claim with an open refund. NEFT has no recall, and the clawback (claimRefundAdjustments, settlementClaims.js:128) only lands if that brand happens to have takings in a future cycle. The docstring claims this is "Repaired rather than merely reported" — it is the flag that is repaired, not the exposure.
suggested_fix: After the updateMany, re-read each transaction whose hold was re-applied and call taintSettlement({transaction, reason}) for any that already carries a settlementId, exactly as requestRefund.js:247 does. Count the taints in the returned health object so a non-zero value is visible.

title: refundAdjustment double-deducts every refund: the refunded transaction was already excluded from the settlement, and its vendorClawback is subtracted again
failure_scenario: Brand B sells claim X: netBill 1000, vendorPromoCost 0, commissionAmount 0. Payment captured Mon. Customer requests a full refund Tue; refund COMPLETES Wed. Golden rule (delayDays*24 >= refund path hours) means X has NOT been settled - by design. Wed sets amountRefunded=1000 and settlementHold=true on X, so X is excluded from every future settlement forever. Brand B also sells claim Y (netBill 1000) the same week. Thursday's build: brandsWithEligibleMoney returns B; claimTransactions captures only Y (grossCollected 1000); claimRefundAdjustments captures the COMPLETED refund on X and subtracts vendorClawback 1000. netPayable = 1000 - 1000 = 0 -> CARRIED_FORWARD. The vendor is paid nothing for Y, a sale that was never refunded. The platform keeps Y's 1000 while the ledger (postRefundEntries.js:91-95 debits VENDOR_PAYABLE by vendorClawback exactly once) still shows the vendor owed 1000. Every completed refund on the platform docks the vendor twice.
suggested_fix: claimRefundAdjustments must only claim refunds whose underlying transaction was actually paid out in an earlier settlement - i.e. join RefundRequest.transactionId to a Transaction with a non-null settlementId whose Settlement reached PAID (or denormalise a `wasSettled`/`clawbackDue` boolean onto RefundRequest at completion time, per the rule-7 pattern). Under the golden rule that set is normally empty, which is the correct answer: the exclusion at settlementClaims.js:66/74 already removes the money. Refunds on never-settled transactions should be claimed and marked as absorbed (settlementId stamped, contributing 0) so they cannot be re-evaluated each cycle.

title: A build that dies between claiming rows and writing totals strands the brand's money forever, with no sweep, no alert, and the idempotencyKey blocking any rebuild
evidence:
buildSettlements.js:172-188 - the unguarded window:
  const [transactions, refunds] = await Promise.all([claimTransactions(...), claimRefundAdjustments(...)]);   // rows now stamped with settlementId
  const totals = computeTotals({ transactions, refunds, settings });
  await Settlement.updateOne({ _id: settlement._id }, { $set: totals });                                       // netPayable first written HERE

Nothing recovers a DRAFT that is in that window:
  services/settlements/settlementJobs.js:320-324 (sweepAbandonedDrafts)
    const holds = await Transaction.countDocuments({ settlementId: draft._id });
    if (holds > 0) continue;                       // <- a draft holding rows is skipped, permanently
  services/settlements/settlementJobs.js:155 (alertLateSettlements)
    netPayable: { $gt: 0 },                        // <- crashed pre-totals draft has netPayable 0, never alerted

And the next build refuses to rebuild the period:
  buildSettlements.js:144  const idempotencyKey = `STL:${brandId}:${periodEnd.toISOString()}`;
  buildSettlements.js:161-166  if (error?.code === DUPLICATE_KEY) return { reused: true };

The documented safety net does not exist: helpers/settlements/settlementClaims.js:180-181 says countClaimedRows is "Used by the stale sweep and by reconcileLedger's stranding invariant", but grep shows its only callers are __tests__/money/settlementClaims.test.js. Likewise models/Settlement.js:233 `index({ isOpen: 1, createdAt: 1 })` is commented "The sweep: settlements still holding rows, oldest first" and no query in services/ or helpers/ ever filters on isOpen for a sweep.
failure_scenario: Brand B's build claims 340 transactions worth 92,400 INR (settlementId stamped). The process is killed (deploy, OOM, pod eviction, a MongoNetworkError on the updateOne) before line 188. Draft D is left: status DRAFT, netPayable 0, holding 340 rows. Next hour's build: brandsWithEligibleMoney no longer returns those rows (settlementId is non-null), and even if it did, Settlement.create throws DUPLICATE_KEY on STL:<B>:<periodEnd> -> `reused: true`. sweepAbandonedDrafts sees holds=340 and skips D. alertLateSettlements filters netPayable > 0 and skips D. No sweep queries isOpen. The 92,400 is invisible to every future cycle for ever, no error and no log - exactly the failure settlementClaims.js:28-35 says the design guards against. Same outcome for the sibling window: a throw out of transitionSettlement (buildSettlements.js:203) after the rows are claimed.
suggested_fix: Give sweepAbandonedDrafts a second branch for non-empty stale DRAFTs: wire up countClaimedRows(draft._id) and, past the stale window, either finish the build (recompute totals from the claimed rows and transition, which is idempotent) or transition to CANCELLED with the key voided - both release the rows through transitionSettlement. Also drop `netPayable: { $gt: 0 }` from alertLateSettlements for DRAFT/ON_HOLD, or replace it with an isOpen-and-holding-rows check so the stranding is at least visible.

title: applyRefundCompletion refuses to claim a FAILED request, so a refund that Razorpay actually created after a local timeout is never recorded — and the webhook reports success
evidence: The conditional claim accepts only `[PROCESSING, ADMIN_APPROVED, ADMIN_OVERRIDE]` (lines 63-71). `FAILED` is absent. executeRefund.js:288-303 writes `status: FAILED` in the catch around `instance.payments.refund(...)` — a catch that fires on a network timeout or 5xx just as readily as on a genuine rejection, i.e. on the exact case where Razorpay did create the refund. When the claim misses, line 85-88 returns `{ applied: false, reason: 'ALREADY_COMPLETED' }`, and handleRazorpayWebhook.js:572-577 turns that into `finish(PROCESSED, "Refund already recorded; nothing to do (redelivery).")`.
failure_scenario: Admin executes a ₹300 refund. Razorpay creates refund rfnd_X and the HTTP response times out. executeRefund's catch writes status=FAILED, attemptCount=1, no razorpayRefundId. Razorpay later sends `refund.processed` for rfnd_X; findRefundRequest matches it via the stamped `notes.refundRequestId` (handleRazorpayWebhook.js:645-653); applyRefundCompletion's filter excludes FAILED, so it does nothing and the webhook is marked PROCESSED with 'already recorded'. Net state: the customer has their ₹300, `Transaction.amountRefunded` is still 0, `refundStatus` is unset, the VoucherClaim is still REDEEMED with `holdsUsageSlot: true` (so the customer is told 'you have already used this offer' for an offer they were refunded), postRefundEntries never runs so the vendor's ledger balance is overstated by the clawback, and the customer gets no refund notification. reconcileRefunds cannot rescue it either — refundJobs.js:206-211 selects only `status: PROCESSING` with `razorpayRefundId: { $type: 'string' }`, and this row is FAILED with no refund id.
suggested_fix: Add REFUND_REQUEST_STATUS.FAILED to the `$in` list at applyRefundCompletion.js:63 (a terminal `refund.processed` from the gateway is authoritative over our local failure record), and stop reporting an unclaimed completion as a benign redelivery — distinguish 'already COMPLETED' from 'status was not claimable' and alert on the latter.

title: findOurRefund adopts a Razorpay refund whose status is `failed`, permanently trapping the request in a PROCESSING↔FAILED loop with the money never re-sent
evidence: `items.find((r) => String(r?.notes?.refundRequestId || "") === String(requestId))` (lines 345-347) matches on the note alone — there is no filter on `r.status`. `fetchMultipleRefund` returns every refund on the payment, including ones Razorpay has marked `failed`. The match feeds straight into `adopt(request, existing, actor, { recovered: true })` (line 271), which sets `status: PROCESSING`, `razorpayRefundId: refund.id`, `failureReason: null` (lines 368-377) and returns without issuing anything. FAILED is a legal entry state (READY includes it, line 218), and the note is the same `String(request._id)` on every attempt (line 284).
failure_scenario: Attempt 1 creates rfnd_X, which Razorpay later fails (bad customer account, closed card). handleRazorpayWebhook.js:535-551 sets the request to FAILED. The admin clicks retry: executeRefund bumps attemptCount to 2, takes the `attemptCount > 1` branch (line 267), findOurRefund returns the *failed* rfnd_X because it carries our note, and adopt marks the request PROCESSING against a dead refund. No new refund is ever issued. reconcileRefunds then picks it up (refundJobs.js:206-211 — PROCESSING with a refund id), `refunds.fetch` reports `failed`, and it writes FAILED back (lines 262-275). Every subsequent retry repeats the cycle forever; the customer's money never goes back and there is no path out short of a manual bank transfer.
suggested_fix: Filter the recovery match to refunds that are still live — `r.status !== 'failed'` (accept `pending`/`processed` only) — so a failed prior attempt falls through to a genuine new `payments.refund()` call. Optionally stamp an attempt-scoped note (`refundRequestId` + `attempt`) so each attempt is individually identifiable.

title: postRefundEntries runs AFTER the request is marked COMPLETED, so any throw permanently loses the ledger reversal — the claim token is already spent and nothing can retry it
evidence: The conditional claim writes `status: COMPLETED` first (lines 60-83) and is the sole idempotency token; on a second entry line 85-88 returns `ALREADY_COMPLETED` and does nothing. Everything that follows is unguarded and un-retryable: `getCustomerConfig()` (line 192), `releaseConsumedPromoOnRefund` (line 194), `postRefundEntries` (line 201), `recordClaimHistory` (line 208). Only the final notification is wrapped in `sendQuietly` (line 236). recordLedgerEntry throws hard on several reachable conditions — `throwError(500, ...)` for a VENDOR_PAYABLE row with no brandId (recordLedgerEntry.js:102-107) and for a non-positive amount (lines 115-117) — and rethrows any non-11000 Mongo error (line 178). This inverts invariant 4 (ledger-first, rows-second on reversals).
failure_scenario: `refund.processed` lands for a ₹810 refund. The request flips to COMPLETED and the Transaction/VoucherClaim/VoucherUsage rows are updated. `getCustomerConfig()` then hits a transient Mongo hiccup (or postRefundEntries hits recordLedgerEntry.js:102 because the VoucherClaim was soft-deleted and `transaction.brandId` is absent). The throw propagates to handleRazorpayWebhook.js:917, which marks the delivery FAILED and pages admins. The admin replays the event: applyRefundCompletion's claim now misses (status is COMPLETED), returns `{ applied: false }`, and the replay reports 'already recorded'. The six reversal rows are never written for that refund — the vendor's VENDOR_PAYABLE balance stays inflated by the full clawback, permanently and silently, and reconcileRefunds cannot see it (it only selects PROCESSING rows).
suggested_fix: Post the ledger rows before flipping the request to COMPLETED (they are already idempotent via `ledger_type_refund_unique`), or keep an explicit `ledgerPostedAt` marker on the RefundRequest and let the reconcile job re-drive completions that are COMPLETED but have no ledger marker, so a mid-way failure is recoverable rather than terminal.

title: A refund processed outside Trydood sets settlementHold but never taints the settlement holding that payment
evidence:
handleRazorpayWebhook.js:595-616 — the no-matching-RefundRequest branch of refund.processed:
```
await Transaction.updateOne({ _id: transaction._id }, { $max: { amountRefunded: cumulative }, $set: { ... settlementHold: true, settlementHoldReason: "Refunded outside Trydood" } });
```
No taintSettlement call follows — the function returns at :620. The dispute branch two hundred lines later does call it (handleRazorpayWebhook.js:729), and requestRefund.js:247 calls it, but this path does not.
That matters because taintSettlement.js:11-18 states the rule: "Once buildSettlements has stamped settlementId on a transaction, setting the hold afterwards has no effect on that settlement at all."
refundJobs.js:178-183 re-applies settlementHold from the reconcile job and likewise never taints.
failure_scenario: Txn T (₹4,000) is claimed into settlement S, which is PENDING_APPROVAL. Someone refunds T from the Razorpay dashboard, or Razorpay auto-refunds a late/duplicate capture. refund.processed arrives with no RefundRequest, so this branch runs: T gets settlementHold: true and amountRefunded 4000, but S keeps needsRevalidation: false and an empty taintedTransactionIds. The admin approves S (approveSettlement.js:88-93 sees a clean flag) and pays. The customer got ₹4,000 back and the vendor got settled for the same sale. Nothing anywhere reports it: reconcileSettlementLedger only compares legs against PAYOUT rows and both agree.
suggested_fix: Call taintSettlement({ transaction, reason: "Refunded outside Trydood" }) after the Transaction.updateOne in this branch (and in refundJobs.js's hold-reapply), exactly as the dispute branch does at line 729.

title: reversePayout: if reversePayoutEntries or the leg updateMany throws, the settlement is already terminal REVERSED and its rows can never be released
evidence:
transitionSettlement.js:87-125 — the status write happens FIRST (`findOneAndUpdate` at :87), then `await beforeRelease(updated)` at :119, then `releaseSettlementClaims` at :124. An exception in beforeRelease propagates and lines 122-127 never run.
paySettlement.js:530-542 puts both the ledger loop and `PayoutLeg.updateMany` inside beforeRelease.
postPayoutEntries.js:115-140 loops legs one at a time with `await recordLedgerEntry(...)` — a throw on leg 3 of 5 leaves 2 credits posted.
constants/settlement.js:125 — `[SETTLEMENT_STATUS.REVERSED]: Object.freeze([])`. Terminal, no exits.
So a retry of POST /reverse re-loads the settlement (paySettlement.js:511), status is REVERSED, and transitionSettlement.js:72-78 throws 422 "A reversed settlement is final and cannot change."
failure_scenario: A multi-leg settlement is reversed and the Mongo write for the second PAYOUT_REVERSAL entry fails (write conflict, replica step-down, validation). The admin gets a 500. The settlement is now REVERSED (terminal), its Transactions and RefundRequests still carry settlementId = S because releaseSettlementClaims never ran, and the reversal is UNDER-stated in the ledger — not over-stated as the comment at postPayoutEntries.js:98-101 claims. Retrying the endpoint 422s; there is no other transition out of REVERSED, so no code path can ever release those rows. The brand's cycle is stranded exactly as invariant 1 describes, and reconcileSettlementLedger skips it (it only queries status: PAID).
suggested_fix: Make the release idempotent and re-runnable: either allow REVERSED -> REVERSED as a no-op repair edge that re-runs beforeRelease + release, or have transitionSettlement run releaseSettlementClaims in a finally/repair sweep keyed on "terminal releasing status still holding rows" (countClaimedRows already exists for exactly this check, settlementClaims.js:182).

title: confirmPayout books the ledger and marks the leg PAID before the settlement transition, leaving a PROCESSING settlement with no confirmable leg and no valid next action
evidence:
paySettlement.js:179-231, in order: leg INITIATED->PAID (:179), `await postPayoutEntries(...)` (:206), then `transitionSettlement({ to: PAID })` (:226).
If line 226 throws, the retry path is paySettlement.js:172-173: `const leg = await currentLeg(settlement._id); if (!leg) throwError(422, "This settlement has no payout leg to confirm.")` — and currentLeg (:442-450) only matches `status: PAYOUT_LEG_STATUS.INITIATED`, which no longer exists.
failPayout has no guard against an already-PAID leg: paySettlement.js:281-292 updates the leg conditionally on INITIATED (so it no-ops) but the settlement transition at :295 to FAILED runs regardless.
ALLOWED[PROCESSING] = [PAID, FAILED] (constants/settlement.js:101-104) — those are the only two doors.
failure_scenario: Two ways in. (a) Non-race: the NEFT is confirmed, the leg is PAID and the PAYOUT ledger row is written, then the transition write fails transiently. The admin retries /confirm and gets 422 "This settlement has no payout leg to confirm" — a dead end with no next action; the only other door is /fail, which writes "the bank rejected it" over a transfer that succeeded and lets retryPayout send a second NEFT. (b) Race: admin A confirms while admin B fails. B's transition PROCESSING->FAILED lands first; A's postPayoutEntries has already written the ₹X PAYOUT row and A's transition then 409s. The settlement is FAILED with a PAID leg, a real UTR and a booked payout — and retryPayout (FAILED->APPROVED) will pay the same money again. reconcileSettlementLedger never sees it because it queries only status: PAID (settlementJobs.js:214).
suggested_fix: Move the transition ahead of the ledger post, or make /confirm recover: if there is no INITIATED leg but a PAID leg exists whose settlement is still PROCESSING, finish the transition instead of 422-ing. And guard failPayout with `paidTotal(settlement._id) > 0` — a settlement with money already out must not be failable.

title: A payout leg records netPayable rather than what was actually transferred, so a split NEFT is booked and closed as a full payout
evidence:
paySettlement.js:104-119 — `PayoutLeg.create({ ..., amount: settlement.netPayable, ... })`. `payload` is declared at :69 and never read. validator/settlements.js:118-127 forces `body: Joi.object({})` on /pay, and validateConfirmPayout (:139-163) accepts utr/mode/reference/paidAt but no amount.
Consequently paidTotal (:459-472) always equals netPayable after the first confirmation, and paySettlement.js:196 `const isFinalLeg = paidSoFar >= round2(settlement.netPayable) - 0.005` is always true — the entire partial branch at :216-224 (`paidSoFar`, `remaining`, `settled: false`) is unreachable.
This directly violates the contract postPayoutEntries.js:24-27 states for its own input: "PAYOUT debits VENDOR_PAYABLE by the amount that actually left. It is not the settlement's netPayable unless the leg carried all of it."
failure_scenario: Settlement netPayable ₹9,00,000; the bank's per-transaction NEFT ceiling forces the admin to send ₹5,00,000 now and ₹4,00,000 later. They confirm the first UTR. The leg is stored at ₹9,00,000, postPayoutEntries books a ₹9,00,000 PAYOUT against VENDOR_PAYABLE, isFinalLeg is true so the RESERVE_HOLD is booked too, the settlement goes PAID, and notifyVendorSettlementPaid tells the vendor the money is on its way. The ₹4,00,000 still owed is on no worklist, and the second UTR has nowhere to be recorded (PAID accepts no further legs — ALLOWED[PAID] = [REVERSED]). reconcileSettlementLedger compares leg total to ledger total and finds them equal, because both are wrong in the same direction.
suggested_fix: Take the actually-transferred amount on /confirm (or on /pay), validate 0 < amount <= netPayable - paidSoFar, store it on the leg, and let startPayout open a further leg while the settlement is PROCESSING and paidSoFar < netPayable. Otherwise remove the split-payout claims and reject any partial transfer explicitly so the admin knows before keying the NEFT.

title: Vendor rejection releases the hold, but an admin override can revive the same refund weeks later — after the money has been settled to the vendor
failure_scenario: Day 1: customer requests ₹810 back; hold on. Day 1: outlet rejects ("we served them"); hold released, isOpen false. Day 4: buildSettlements claims the row (settlementClaims.js:113) and the brand is paid — legitimately, by the current rules. Day 10: the customer escalates, the admin overrides the rejection with a reason; approveRefundAsAdmin sets ADMIN_OVERRIDE/isOpen true and nothing re-applies the hold or taints anything. executeRefund refunds ₹810 to the customer out of Trydood's own float. repairMissingHolds (refundJobs.js:167-195) re-applies settlementHold up to 30 minutes later, but the row already carries a settlementId, and taintSettlement.js:12-15 documents that a hold on a claimed row "has no effect on that settlement at all". Recovery depends entirely on the brand having a future settlement for claimRefundAdjustments (settlementClaims.js:128-137) to deduct vendorClawback from — a churned or seasonal brand has none, and the golden rule that is supposed to make this impossible does not cover an override with no time bound on it.
suggested_fix: Either (a) re-apply settlementHold and call taintSettlement inside approveRefundAsAdmin whenever isOverride is true, before returning; or (b) do not release the hold on VENDOR_REJECTED at all — hold it until the override window has closed — since VENDOR_REJECTED is by construction not a terminal state. Additionally, refuse an override (or force the MANUAL_BANK/clawback path) when the transaction's settlementId points at a PAID settlement.

title: Nothing detects or repairs a hold with no open refund behind it — the inverse of unheldRefunds is missing and unsettledCaptures deliberately hides it
evidence:
getPaymentHealth.js:236-250 asks only one direction — open refund whose payment is NOT held:
  RefundRequest.aggregate([{ $match: { isOpen: true, isDeleted: false } }, { $lookup: ... }, { $match: { "payment.settlementHold": { $ne: true } } }, { $count: "total" }])
There is no counterpart query for a transaction with settlementHold: true and no open RefundRequest / unresolved dispute.

And the one counter that could have caught it excludes held rows on purpose — :151-158:
  Transaction.countDocuments({ ...claimFilter, verified: true, settlementId: null, settlementHold: { $ne: true }, createdAt: { $lte: now - 10 days } })
So a permanently held payment is invisible in `unsettledCaptures` as well.

The repair job is one-directional too: refundJobs.js:167-195 only ever writes settlementHold: true. docs/vendor_settlement_plan.md:529 specifies this exact missing check as reconcileLedger's 8th invariant ("koi transaction settlementHold: true par N din se zyada na baithe bina kisi khuli refund request ya khule dispute ke → WARNING"); services/settlements/settlementJobs.js:210-284 implements no such check.
failure_scenario: rejectRefundAsVendor writes the status at decideRefund.js:176 and releases the hold at :192 — two separate round trips, exactly the shape repairMissingHolds exists to repair in the other direction. The process is restarted (deploy, OOM) between them. The RefundRequest is now VENDOR_REJECTED / isOpen: false and the Transaction still has settlementHold: true. `unheldRefunds` does not match it (the refund is not open). `unsettledCaptures` filters it out (`settlementHold: { $ne: true }`). No job repairs it. The vendor's money for that claim is out of every settlement for ever and the health page reports OK. Same outcome for the WON-chargeback case above, and for any hold left by a partial refund.
suggested_fix: Add a `strandedHolds` signal to getPaymentHealth: Transaction.countDocuments over settlementHold: true, settlementId: null, older than N days, with no RefundRequest isOpen:true and no unresolved dispute — and grade it ATTENTION (it is money silently frozen). Return the ids, not just a count, so an admin has something to act on, and pair it with the admin release endpoint from the first finding. Extending repairMissingHolds to also clear holds whose reason no longer applies is the alternative, but detection plus an explicit human release is safer here.

title: A completed PARTIAL refund excludes the payment from settlement for ever, while the clawback for the refunded part is still deducted — the vendor is docked twice
evidence:
applyRefundCompletion.js:112-137 runs for every completed refund, partial or full:
  $max: { amountRefunded: cumulative },
  $set: { refundStatus: isFullyRefunded ? COMPLETED : PARTIAL, ..., settlementHold: true, settlementHoldReason: `Refunded (${claimed._id})` }
`isFullyRefunded` is computed at :110 but is not consulted for the hold.

Eligibility then blocks the row on both counts — settlementClaims.js:66 `settlementHold: false` and :74 `amountRefunded: { $lte: 0 }` — and nothing ever releases either (releaseSettlementHold is not called on COMPLETED, by design: constants/refund.js:81-85).

Meanwhile the deduction is still taken: settlementClaims.js:128-137 claims every COMPLETED RefundRequest for the brand regardless of whether the underlying payment was ever settled, and buildSettlements.js:248-251 subtracts `split.vendorClawback` from the brand's netPayable. calculateRefundSplit.js:151-169 computes that clawback pro-rata for a partial (`ratio = vendorPortion / vendorSidePaid`).
failure_scenario: ₹810 claim, never settled yet (well inside T+3). Customer gets a ₹300 partial refund; it completes. Transaction: amountRefunded 300, refundStatus PARTIAL, isRefunded false, settlementHold true, settlementId still null. That row is now excluded from every future cycle, so the vendor never receives their share of the ₹510 we are still holding for that sale. On top of that, the COMPLETED RefundRequest is claimed by the next settlement and its vendorClawback (~₹280 of vendor-side money) is subtracted from that cycle's netPayable, taken out of other sales. Net effect: the vendor is charged for the refunded ₹300 and paid nothing for the ₹510 they did deliver. The settlement statement balances internally, so nothing flags it.
suggested_fix: A partially refunded payment still owes the vendor its remainder. Either (a) settle the row net — let it stay eligible with `amountRefunded > 0` and have computeTotals use `netBill - netBillRefund` for it, dropping the separate clawback for refunds whose transaction has not previously been settled; or (b) keep the exclusion but credit the remainder through a `claimRefundAdjustments`-style positive adjustment. Only the full-refund case (`isFullyRefunded === true`) justifies the permanent hold at :133.

title: Admin override of a VENDOR_REJECTED refund hits the (transactionId,isOpen) unique index and is permanently impossible once the customer re-requests
evidence:
executeRefund.js:85-101 —
  const updated = await RefundRequest.findOneAndUpdate(
    { _id: request._id, status: { $in: ADMIN_CAN_DECIDE } },   // includes VENDOR_REJECTED, VENDOR_TIMEOUT
    { $set: { status: isOverride ? ADMIN_OVERRIDE : ADMIN_APPROVED, ..., isOpen: true } },

models/RefundRequest.js:242-249 —
  refundRequestSchema.index({ transactionId: 1, isOpen: 1 },
    { unique: true, partialFilterExpression: { isOpen: true } });

No try/catch for DUPLICATE_KEY anywhere in executeRefund.js or decideRefund.js (grep for DUPLICATE_KEY/11000 shows only requestRefund.js:205 in the whole refund subsystem).

requestRefund.js has nothing that refuses a re-request after a rejection: REFUNDABLE_CLAIM_STATUSES (line 38-41) still matches, and assertRefundAllowance only counts VENDOR_REJECTED toward maxRejectedPerWindow (default 3, constants/customer.js:266).
failure_scenario: Customer requests ₹810 on transaction T (request A, isOpen=true, hold on). Vendor rejects within the hour: decideRefund.js:184 sets isOpen=false and releaseSettlementHold lifts the hold. The transaction now has no open request. The customer, still inside the 24h window, requests again — assertRefundAllowance passes (0 other open, 1 rejection < 3), the partial unique index is free, so request B is created with isOpen=true. An admin then opens the worklist and overrides request A (VENDOR_REJECTED is in ADMIN_CAN_DECIDE, executeRefund.js:32-36). The $set writes isOpen:true on A, colliding with B on refund_open_per_transaction_unique. The driver throws E11000, which middlewares/errorHandler.js:12-16 renders as HTTP 422 "68f1a… is already registered for transactionId". The override can never succeed — every retry produces the same message, and neither the admin nor the customer has any next action. The same collision blocks rejectRefundAsAdmin's sibling path via approveRefundAsAdmin for VENDOR_TIMEOUT rows.
suggested_fix: Refuse a new request in requestRefund while any prior request on the same transaction is still admin-actionable (VENDOR_REJECTED / VENDOR_TIMEOUT), or catch DUPLICATE_KEY in approveRefundAsAdmin and return a 409 naming the newer open request so the admin can act on that one instead.

title: Partial refunds that never reach the full amount claw back more from the vendor than the vendor was ever paid — the pro-rata ratio is not clamped to 1
failure_scenario:
Payment of ₹810 = netBill ₹800 + convenienceFee ₹10, allowPartial true (the default, constants/customer.js:226). Two ways to reach the same loss:
(a) Single request of ₹805: isFullRefund is false (805 < 810−0.005), so convenienceFeeRefund=0, vendorPortion=805, vendorSidePaid=800, ratio=1.00625, netBillRefund=805, vendorClawback=805. Verified by direct evaluation.
(b) ₹300 then ₹505 (each individually under 800): first split claws 300, second claws 505 — 805 total.
Either way the vendor is docked ₹805 against ₹800 they were ever owed; the extra ₹5 is exactly the convenience fee, which the design says is NOT returned on a partial. Trydood keeps its ₹10 fee and takes another ₹5 out of the vendor's settlement. The split passes every assertion and is frozen onto the RefundRequest, so postRefundEntries and buildSettlements both act on the wrong number.
suggested_fix: Base the ratio on what is left of the vendor side, not on all of it: ratio = vendorPortion / (vendorSidePaid − priorVendorSideRefunded), and refuse a partial whose vendorPortion exceeds the remaining vendor side rather than letting ratio exceed 1.

title: repairMissingHolds silently stops at 500 open refunds and never reaches the rest — the hold-repair guarantee has a permanent blind spot
failure_scenario: Steady-state backlog of 600 open refund requests (REQUESTED + VENDOR_TIMEOUT + FAILED all count as open, constants/refund.js:57-66; FAILED rows in particular never leave the open set until an admin retries). Request #501 in scan order is one whose requestRefund process died between RefundRequest.create (requestRefund.js:184) and the Transaction.updateOne that sets settlementHold (requestRefund.js:228). Every run of the job selects the same first 500 rows — they stay open, so the window never advances past them — and #501 is never even a candidate. Its transaction stays settlementHold:false, buildSettlements claims it (helpers/settlements/settlementClaims.js:66 filters settlementHold:false), the vendor is paid at T+3, and the refund then has nothing to come out of. Nothing errors and nothing logs.
suggested_fix: Put the missing-hold condition in the query itself — aggregate/lookup open requests whose transaction has settlementHold != true — or page the scan with a cursor on _id so successive runs cover the whole open set instead of re-reading the same 500.

title: ADMIN_OVERRIDE is missing from REFUND_OPEN_STATUSES, so every API surface reports an override-approved refund as closed while it still awaits payout
evidence:
constants/refund.js:57-66 — REFUND_OPEN_STATUSES = [REQUESTED, VENDOR_APPROVED, VENDOR_TIMEOUT, ADMIN_APPROVED, PROCESSING, FAILED]. ADMIN_OVERRIDE is absent, although executeRefund.js:89-97 writes `status: ADMIN_OVERRIDE` together with `isOpen: true`, and executeRefund.js:213-221 lists ADMIN_OVERRIDE in READY as a state that still has to be paid.

Every read path then contradicts the stored flag:
- helpers/refunds/buildRefundReadPipeline.js:175 — `isOpen: REFUND_OPEN_STATUSES.includes(request.status)` overwrites the projected stored value (line 88) with `false`.
- services/refunds/executeRefund.js:403 — same expression in `present()`, so the admin's own approve response says `isOpen: false`.
- models/RefundRequest.js:226-228 — `pre("save")` derives `this.isOpen = REFUND_OPEN_STATUSES.includes(this.status)`, i.e. the schema itself agrees ADMIN_OVERRIDE is closed.
failure_scenario: Vendor ignores a refund -> escalateStaleRefunds sets VENDOR_TIMEOUT -> admin calls PATCH /refunds/admin/:id/approve with an overrideReason. The row is stored `status: ADMIN_OVERRIDE, isOpen: true` and still needs PATCH /admin/:id/pay. The 200 response returns `isOpen: false` (executeRefund.js:403), and GET /refunds (any role) returns `isOpen: false, canDecide: false, canWithdraw: false` for it (buildRefundReadPipeline.js:175, 181-190). A panel that renders its pay/worklist affordance from the returned `isOpen` drops the row: nobody presses pay, no sweep watches ADMIN_OVERRIDE (escalateStaleRefunds only matches REQUESTED, refundJobs.js:49), and the customer sits on statusLabel "Approved by Trydood" (constants/refund.js:128) with money that never moves and the vendor's settlementHold on for ever behind it. Latent second failure: because the pre-save hook derives the same wrong value, the first time any code path loads such a doc and calls .save(), the stored isOpen flips to false, freeing the partialFilterExpression `{isOpen: true}` unique index (models/RefundRequest.js:242-249) and letting the customer file a second open refund against the same payment.
suggested_fix: Add REFUND_REQUEST_STATUS.ADMIN_OVERRIDE to REFUND_OPEN_STATUSES in constants/refund.js:57. It satisfies the existing invariant test (refundRequest.test.js:188) since it is not in REFUND_HOLD_RELEASING_STATUSES. Consider adding an assertion that every status written with `isOpen: true` by a service is a member of the list.

title: A vendor approving or declining a refund sends the customer nothing — and the admin path deliberately skips its notification believing the vendor path already sent one
failure_scenario: Normal happy path: customer requests a refund (notified, requestRefund.js:278), vendor approves via PATCH /refunds/:id/approve. No message is sent. Admin then approves — isOverride is false because VENDOR_APPROVED is not in OVERRIDE_FROM (executeRefund.js:38-41, 73), so executeRefund.js:123 skips the notification on the stated assumption that the vendor step already sent one. The customer therefore hears nothing at all between "refund requested" and the final notifyClaimRefunded, which only fires days later when Razorpay settles (applyRefundCompletion.js:236). Worse on the decline: the vendor rejects with a note, the request goes terminal, the settlement hold is released, and the customer is never told — they discover it only by re-opening the app, with no note, no reason and no next action.
suggested_fix: Call `await sendQuietly(() => notifyCustomerRefundApproved({ request: updated }), "customer refund approved by vendor")` at the end of approveRefundAsVendor, and `notifyCustomerRefundRejected` at the end of rejectRefundAsVendor. Either that, or remove the `if (isOverride)` guard in executeRefund.js:123 so the admin approval is what notifies — but the comment there must then stop claiming the vendor path already did.

title: repairMissingHolds scans a non-draining set with .limit(500) and no sort, so past 500 open refunds the tail never gets its settlement hold repaired
failure_scenario: Open refunds accumulate without bound: FAILED stays isOpen forever until an admin retries (constants/refund.js:63-65, executeRefund.js:291-302), and VENDOR_APPROVED / ADMIN_APPROVED are watched by no sweep at all (getPaymentHealth.js:203-222 documents this). Once the collection holds more than 500 such rows, a refund created at position 501+ whose `Transaction.updateOne` at requestRefund.js:228-237 did not land — the process died between `RefundRequest.create` (line 184) and the hold write — is never repaired. buildSettlements' eligibility predicate (helpers/settlements/settlementClaims.js:66 `settlementHold: false`) then matches it, the vendor is paid for a claim that is about to be refunded, and the refund has nothing to come out of. Silent: getPaymentHealth.js:236-250 counts it, but reconcileRefunds reports `holdsRepaired: 0` and no error is raised.
suggested_fix: Make the sweep drain: either iterate with a cursor / `_id: { $gt: lastId }` pagination until exhausted, or invert it to a bounded query on the wrong side — `Transaction.updateMany({ _id: { $in: <open refund txn ids> }, settlementHold: { $ne: true } })` driven by a paged scan. At minimum add `.sort({ createdAt: -1 })` so newly created rows (the ones actually at risk of a dropped second round trip) are covered rather than starved.

title: COMMISSION is never posted at capture, yet a COMMISSION reversal is posted on refund
evidence:
grep -rn "COMMISSION" --include=*.js (excluding tests) returns only:
  constants/ledger.js:81   COMMISSION: "COMMISSION",
  constants/ledger.js:145  [LEDGER_ENTRY_TYPE.COMMISSION]: { account: PLATFORM_REVENUE, direction: CREDIT }
  helpers/ledger/postRefundEntries.js:124 the reversal

Nothing writes the forward entry. constants/ledger.js:80-81 claims "Written when a settlement is PAID", but services/settlements/paySettlement.js:206 calls only postPayoutEntries, whose plan (postPayoutEntries.js:60-78) is PAYOUT + RESERVE_HOLD. postCaptureEntries.js:57-97 has no COMMISSION row either.

Meanwhile buildSettlements.js:257-258 subtracts it from what the vendor is actually paid:
  const beforeReserve = round2(grossCollected - vendorPromoCost - commissionAmount - refundAdjustment);
failure_scenario:
Set settlement.commissionPercent to a non-zero value (admin-settable: validator/settings.js:180, models/Setting.js:424). Claim netBill 800, commission 5% = 40, vendorPromoCost 15.
(a) Vendor side: capture credits 800 and debits 15 -> ledger says the brand is owed 785. The settlement pays netPayable = 800 - 15 - 40 = 745. PAYOUT debits 745. The ledger balance settles at +40 forever, per claim. constants/ledger.js:12-13 states the vendor's balance IS the sum of their VENDOR_PAYABLE rows and Settlement.netPayable is "a cache" — here the authoritative figure is the wrong one, permanently overstated by the whole commission book.
(b) Platform side: on refund, postRefundEntries.js:124-129 DEBITs PLATFORM_REVENUE by commissionReversal (40) for a credit that was never made. getPlatformTotals (getVendorBalance.js:186) reports revenue = credited - debited, so a refunded claim pushes reported platform revenue 40 below where it should be — the same class of sign error the docblock at getVendorBalance.js:162-173 says the ledger exists to make impossible.
suggested_fix: Either post the forward COMMISSION pair at capture (DEBIT VENDOR_PAYABLE + CREDIT PLATFORM_REVENUE by pricing.commissionAmount, added to ONCE_PER_TRANSACTION_TYPES), or stop posting the reversal at postRefundEntries.js:124-129 and fold commissionReversal back into the vendor clawback. Half the pair is strictly worse than neither half. Gate the settings change behind whichever is implemented.

title: TAX_COLLECTED is never reversed on a refund — TAX_PAYABLE keeps GST that was handed back to the customer
evidence:
postCaptureEntries.js:93-96 books it:
  { entryType: LEDGER_ENTRY_TYPE.TAX_COLLECTED, amount: pricing?.gstAmount, ... }   // CREDIT TAX_PAYABLE

The refund plan (postRefundEntries.js:89-142) has six rows: COLLECTION, VENDOR_PROMO_SHARE, CONVENIENCE_FEE, PLATFORM_PROMO_COST, COMMISSION, GATEWAY_FEE. There is no TAX_COLLECTED row.

But the tax IS returned to the customer — calculateRefundSplit.js:137 and :223:
  const taxRefund = isFullRefund ? taxOnTop : 0;
  ... split.convenienceFeeRefund + split.taxRefund   // part of totalRefund
failure_scenario:
Turn GST on (tax.isGstEnabled, admin-settable: validator/settings.js:109, models/Setting.js:259) in the default exclusive mode. Fee 10, 18% -> pricing.gstAmount = pricing.taxOnTop = 1.80, customer pays 811.80.
Capture: TAX_PAYABLE +1.80.
Full refund: the customer is sent back 811.80, which includes the 1.80 of GST (calculateRefundSplit.js:137). Ledger rows posted for the refund total only 810.00 across VENDOR_PAYABLE/PLATFORM_REVENUE/PLATFORM_COST. TAX_PAYABLE is untouched.
Result: 1.80 of cash left the building with no ledger row on the other side, and TAX_PAYABLE permanently claims we owe the government GST on a supply that was cancelled. getPlatformTotals (getVendorBalance.js:126) reports the same inflated TAX_PAYABLE. On every refunded claim, forever, with no error and no log.
suggested_fix: Add a seventh row to the refund plan: { entryType: TAX_COLLECTED, amount: split.taxRefund, account: TAX_PAYABLE, direction: DEBIT }. It is already covered by ledger_type_refund_unique, and it is skipped automatically while GST is off because split.taxRefund is 0.

title: releaseJobLock clears the lock without checking ownership, so a lapsed instance destroys the live lease of the instance that took over
failure_scenario: Instance A runs buildSettlements. One heartbeat throws on a transient Mongo error — renewJobLock catches it and returns false (jobLock.js:85-88) — and the 15-minute lease (JOB_LOCK_LEASE_MINUTES, constants/job.js:30) lapses. Instance B's next tick acquires the expired lock (jobLock.js:47 matches on expiresAt <= now) and starts buildSettlements. Instance A then finishes and its `finally` (jobs/index.js:271) calls releaseJobLock, which unconditionally writes lockedBy:null and expiresAt:now — deleting B's live lease while B is still mid-run. Any instance's next tick, including A's, now acquires cleanly and starts a third concurrent run of the same money job. The cross-process guarantee the runner documents at jobs/index.js:46-55 is gone precisely in the failure mode it was built for, and getJobHealth's isRunning (getJobHealth.js:82-84) reports false while two runs are in flight.
suggested_fix: Split the write: apply the health fields with the unscoped `{_id: name}` filter, and clear `lockedBy`/`expiresAt` in a second update scoped to `{ _id: name, lockedBy: INSTANCE_ID }` so a lapsed owner cannot release someone else's lease.

title: A DRAFT settlement that dies after claiming rows but before writing totals is invisible to both settlement safety nets and strands its rows for ever
failure_scenario: buildForBrand creates the DRAFT shell (buildSettlements.js:148), claimTransactions stamps settlementId on the brand's rows (settlementClaims.js:113), and the process is killed before Settlement.updateOne({$set: totals}) at buildSettlements.js:188 — a deploy, an OOM, a Mongo blip. The settlement now sits in DRAFT for ever with netPayable 0 and N transactions claimed. sweepAbandonedDrafts refuses to touch it (holds > 0); alertLateSettlements never selects it (netPayable is 0). Its idempotencyKey `STL:{brandId}:{periodEnd}` still occupies the period, so every future build of that day returns `{reused: true}` (buildSettlements.js:161-167). Every future cycle's eligibility predicate asks for `settlementId: null` (settlementClaims.js:57), so the claimed rows are invisible to every cycle from then on. No error, no alert, no log — precisely the silent stranding constants/settlement.js:131-152 says must never happen, and the vendor discovers it weeks later as a figure that never arrived.
suggested_fix: Give sweepAbandonedDrafts a second branch for a stale DRAFT that IS holding rows: alert an admin naming the settlement and the claimed row count (the ledger cannot see this, so nothing else will), or release the rows and cancel through transitionSettlement so the next build rebuilds the period cleanly. At minimum drop `netPayable: { $gt: 0 }` for DRAFT in alertLateSettlements so an unpriced stranded draft is reachable.

title: alertLateSettlements bumps the sent-counter before sending and swallows the delivery failure, so a mail outage silently kills the only overdue alert a settlement will ever get
failure_scenario: The mail/push provider is down for one hour. Every settlement that crosses `notReceivedAlertHours` (default 96) during that hour is claimed, has overdueAlertsSent set to 1, and its notification throws inside sendQuietly — logged to stdout and discarded. The filter `$lt: 1` means those settlements are permanently excluded from every future run of the job. Money owed past the window we promised, and the design goal stated at settlementJobs.js:122-124 — "so the first person to know is not the vendor waiting for it" — is defeated with no trace. releaseJobLock then writes `lastResult: { checked: N, alerted: N }` and `lastSuccessfulRunAt` (jobLock.js:147-151), so the health record reports a clean run that alerted N settlements when it alerted none.
suggested_fix: Send first, then bump the counter only on a delivered notification — or have sendQuietly return a truthy/falsy result and roll the counter back (or leave it unbumped) when the send returned null, so the next tick retries. Either way, return a `deliveryFailures` count from the job so a stream of them shows up in JobLock.lastResult instead of reading as success.

title: repairMissingHolds scans the first 500 open refunds with no sort, and permanently-open FAILED refunds accumulate at the head and starve every newer one
failure_scenario: A gateway incident (or a run of bad customer bank accounts) leaves 500+ RefundRequests with isOpen:true — FAILED ones that nobody has retried, plus VENDOR_TIMEOUT ones waiting on an admin. Without a sort, the planner returns the same first 500 every run (the partial index on {transactionId:1, isOpen:1}, RefundRequest.js:242, gives a stable transactionId ordering), so those long-lived rows occupy the whole window permanently. A refund requested today whose settlementHold write was lost — the exact case this function exists for, refundJobs.js:157-165 — is at position 501 and its hold is never re-applied by any run of the job. Its transaction stays eligible, buildSettlements claims and pays it, and the invariant the docstring calls "the guarantee the rest of the design rests on" (refundJobs.js:198) is not enforced for it.
suggested_fix: Make the query targeted rather than truncated: select only rows that are actually wrong, e.g. drive it from Transaction (`settlementHold: { $ne: true }` joined to open requests) or paginate with a `_id` cursor across runs so the whole open set is covered. If a limit stays, sort by `updatedAt: 1` or `_id: 1` with a stored high-water mark so the tail is reachable.

title: resumeIncompleteSettlements takes 50 stranded transactions with no sort and no failure backoff, so a permanently failing row blocks every newer one for ever
failure_scenario: One stranded transaction fails settleVoucherClaimPayment deterministically — for instance the VoucherUsage E11000 branch at settleVoucherClaimPayment.js:250-261, whose fallback re-creates a row with the same `voucherClaimId` against the unconditionally-unique `voucherUsage_claim_unique` index (VoucherUsage.js:164-167) and throws again uncaught; or a claim whose pricing subdocument is missing. It never reaches COMPLETE, so it stays in the candidate set. With no sort the planner returns the same 50 rows each tick, so once 50 such rows accumulate the window is permanently full and every transaction stranded after that point is never resumed. Each one is, in this job's own words (claimJobs.js:201-203), "a customer who paid and a vendor who has not been credited" — and the CRITICAL admin notification is deduped hourly on `RESUME_FAILED:{hour}` (claimJobs.js:205), so it reports a count, never which rows, and never that the queue has stopped moving.
suggested_fix: Add `.sort({ verifiedAt: 1 })` plus an attempt counter on the transaction, skipping rows past N attempts into an explicit quarantine that is alerted on by id. Add a partial index on `{ settlementStage: 1, verifiedAt: 1 }` scoped to purpose VOUCHER_CLAIM so the 15-minute sweep stops scanning the collection.

title: A partially refunded payment's remaining vendor balance is permanently unpayable - settlementHold and amountRefunded both stay set and nothing ever settles the residual
evidence:
helpers/settlements/settlementClaims.js:68-74
   * Tested on the **amount**, not on `isRefunded`.
   * A partial refund leaves `isRefunded: false` while real money has already
   * gone back, so a boolean test would settle the vendor for the full sale.
  amountRefunded: { $lte: 0 },
plus settlementClaims.js:66  settlementHold: false

Both are set permanently on a partial completion:
  helpers/refunds/applyRefundCompletion.js:118  $max: { amountRefunded: cumulative }
  helpers/refunds/applyRefundCompletion.js:126-134
    refundStatus: isFullyRefunded ? COMPLETED : REFUND_STATUS.PARTIAL,
    settlementHold: true,
    settlementHoldReason: `Refunded (${claimed._id})`,
helpers/refunds/releaseSettlementHold.js is never called for COMPLETED - releaseSettlementHold.js:17-19 states "`FAILED` and `COMPLETED` deliberately do not".

No query anywhere settles a residual: grep for amountRefunded across services/settlements and helpers/settlements returns only the two `$lte: 0` exclusions and one projection in taintSettlement.js:81.
failure_scenario: Customer pays 810 for claim X (netBill 800, convenienceFee 10). They get a partial refund of 200. applyRefundCompletion writes amountRefunded=200, refundStatus=PARTIAL, settlementHold=true. X now fails both settlementHold: false and amountRefunded: { $lte: 0 }, so it is excluded from every settlement for ever. The vendor supplied 800 of food and 600 of it was never refunded, but they are paid 0 for X - and, per the finding above, a further 200 vendorClawback is deducted from their other takings. The comment at settlementClaims.js:70-73 correctly identifies that settling the full sale is wrong, but the code's alternative is settling none of it, with no residual path.
suggested_fix: Settle the residual rather than excluding the row: keep the exclusion for settlementHold (dispute/open refund) but let a fully-decided partial through and credit (netBill - netBillRefund) - vendorPromoCost residual - commission residual, using the frozen RefundRequest.split figures already on the row. Concretely: release settlementHold on a COMPLETED partial once no other refund is open and no dispute is live, and change the amount test from `amountRefunded: { $lte: 0 }` to a per-row residual computation in computeTotals.

title: The eligibility scan is a full collection scan of every voucher payment ever captured - the sparse settlementId index cannot serve `settlementId: null`
evidence:
models/Transaction.js:463-464
  // buildSettlements' eligibility scan.
  transactionSchema.index({ settlementId: 1 }, { sparse: true });

A sparse index omits documents where the field is missing, so MongoDB's planner will not use it for an equality-on-null predicate (it would return incomplete results). Both hot queries use exactly that predicate:
  services/settlements/buildSettlements.js:124-134 (brandsWithEligibleMoney)
    Transaction.distinct("brandId", { ...buildTransactionFilter({purpose: VOUCHER_CLAIM}), verified: true, status: CAPTURED, settlementId: null, settlementHold: false, amountRefunded: { $lte: 0 }, verifiedAt: {...}, fundsReceivedAt: {...}, isDeleted: false })
  helpers/settlements/settlementClaims.js:46-91 + :113 (the updateMany)

The only usable index left is models/Transaction.js:456 `{ purpose: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }` - prefix purpose+status. That scans every CAPTURED VOUCHER_CLAIM row ever written; the settled ones (the growing majority) cannot be excluded by any index. distinct() also has no .limit() and no bound on the returned brand array (buildSettlements.js:123).

jobs/index.js:186-188 runs this every 60 minutes, i.e. 24 full scans of the lifetime transaction history per day.
failure_scenario: Year two, 4 million captured voucher claims of which ~30k are unsettled. Every hour, brandsWithEligibleMoney examines all 4 million index entries plus fetches to evaluate settlementId/settlementHold/amountRefunded, then claimTransactions repeats the same scan once per eligible brand (10k brands -> 10k more scans, sequentially, in the same job tick). The build blows through its JobLock heartbeat, the tick overlaps the next, and settlement latency grows linearly with lifetime volume rather than with unsettled volume. The comment at Transaction.js:463 asserts an index serves this scan, so nobody looks.
suggested_fix: Denormalise the lock into a boolean the way the codebase already does elsewhere (VoucherClaim.holdsUsageSlot, LedgerEntry.isOncePerTransaction) - e.g. `isSettleable`/`awaitingSettlement`, set true at capture and false when settlementId is stamped or a hold goes on - and add a partial compound index `{ brandId: 1, verifiedAt: 1 }` with `partialFilterExpression: { awaitingSettlement: true, purpose: 'VOUCHER_CLAIM' }`. That makes both the distinct and the updateMany proportional to unsettled rows. Replace the distinct with an aggregation that both groups by brand and caps the batch.

title: refund.failed has no status guard and will flip a COMPLETED request back to FAILED, re-opening a refund whose money already landed
evidence: The REFUND_CREATED branch guards its write — `RefundRequest.updateOne({ _id: request._id, status: { $ne: REFUND_REQUEST_STATUS.COMPLETED } }, ...)` (line 517). The REFUND_FAILED branch immediately below has no such clause: `RefundRequest.updateOne({ _id: request._id }, { $set: { status: FAILED, failedAt, failureReason, isOpen: true } })` (lines 537-551). Nothing checks the current status.
failure_scenario: Razorpay's deliveries for one refund arrive out of order (each event has its own event id, so the WebhookEvent dedupe at line 899 does not collapse them). `refund.processed` is applied and the request reaches COMPLETED with ledger rows posted and the customer notified. A delayed retry of `refund.failed` for the same refund then lands and unconditionally rewrites the row to FAILED / isOpen: true. The request reappears in the admin retry worklist and the customer's status label flips from 'Refunded' to 'Refund failed — we are on it' (constants/refund.js:131) for money that is already in their account. If the admin retries, executeRefund takes the FAILED entry (line 218), adopts the processed refund, and puts it back to PROCESSING; reconcileRefunds then re-runs applyRefundCompletion, which now claims the PROCESSING row and fires a second 'your refund is done' notification (applyRefundCompletion.js:236-245) plus a duplicate REFUNDED claim-history row.
suggested_fix: Add the same guard the created branch uses — `{ _id: request._id, status: { $ne: REFUND_REQUEST_STATUS.COMPLETED } }` — so a late or out-of-order `refund.failed` cannot un-complete a refund that already settled.

title: `refundStatus` / `isRefunded` are $set from a possibly-stale cumulative while only the number is $max-protected, so an out-of-order refund.processed walks a fully-refunded payment back to PARTIAL
evidence: `$max: { amountRefunded: cumulative }` (line 118) is monotonic, but the derived fields sitting beside it in the same `$set` are not: `refundStatus: isFullyRefunded ? COMPLETED : PARTIAL`, `isRefunded: isFullyRefunded`, `latestRefundRequestId: claimed._id` (lines 126-132), where `isFullyRefunded = cumulative >= round2(paidAmount) - 0.005` (line 110) is computed from *this* event's snapshot. The doc comment at lines 115-117 claims the `$max` makes the write safe 'under redelivery and out-of-order delivery alike' — that is true of the number only.
failure_scenario: Payment of ₹810 refunded in two parts: RR-A ₹300 (Razorpay stamps amount_refunded=300 on A's payload) then RR-B ₹510 (amount_refunded=810). B's `refund.processed` is delivered first: transaction becomes amountRefunded=810, refundStatus=COMPLETED, isRefunded=true, claim REFUNDED. A's delayed first delivery then arrives with gatewayTotalRefunded=300; RR-A is still PROCESSING so the claim succeeds, `$max` correctly keeps 810, but the same update writes `refundStatus: PARTIAL`, `isRefunded: false` and points `latestRefundRequestId` at the older, smaller request. The transaction now reports itself as partially refunded with ₹0 outstanding — every read path that keys on those fields (buildClaimReadPipeline.js:150 projects refundStatus; the admin/vendor refund reports) is wrong, and the migrateRefundFoundation backfill exists precisely to repair this class of row.
suggested_fix: Derive the flags from the value that actually won the `$max`: re-read the transaction after the update (or use a pipeline update so `refundStatus`/`isRefunded` are computed from `$max` of the stored and incoming totals inside the same write), and guard `latestRefundRequestId` so it only advances to a later completion.

title: sweepStalePayouts silently skips the orphan-leg state it exists to catch
evidence:
settlementJobs.js:84-100 — the stale INITIATED legs are joined against `Settlement.find({ _id: { $in: ... }, status: SETTLEMENT_STATUS.PROCESSING })`, then `const settlement = byId.get(String(leg.settlementId)); if (!settlement) continue;`.
startPayout's own comment at paySettlement.js:127-134 promises the opposite: "A crash in between leaves an APPROVED settlement with an INITIATED leg — visible, and the sweep can resolve it."
Also note settlementJobs.js:72-80 caps the scan with `.limit(200)` and, because a skipped leg is never mutated or marked, the same 200 oldest legs are re-read every run — a growing backlog of unresolvable legs starves newer ones out of the window.
failure_scenario: The process dies (or transitionSettlement 409s) between PayoutLeg.create at paySettlement.js:104 and the PROCESSING transition at :135. The settlement is APPROVED, the leg is INITIATED. Six hours later sweepStalePayouts finds the leg, cannot find a PROCESSING settlement for it, and `continue`s — no alert is ever raised, so nobody learns whether that NEFT was keyed in. Meanwhile a second /pay call counts the orphan (countDocuments at :97 has no status filter) and opens legNumber 2, so the leg numbering permanently reflects an attempt no one can resolve.
suggested_fix: Widen the join to APPROVED and FAILED settlements and alert with a different message ("leg opened but the settlement never moved — did this NEFT go out?"), or stamp a swept marker on the leg so the .limit(200) window advances instead of re-reading the same unresolvable head.

title: repairMissingHolds silently repairs only the oldest 500 open refunds — and FAILED refunds stay open for ever, so the backlog only grows
failure_scenario: Once a platform accumulates 500 open refunds — FAILED ones alone accumulate monotonically — the natural-order scan returns the 500 oldest and never reaches anything newer. A customer files a refund at that point and the process dies between RefundRequest.create (requestRefund.js:184) and the settlementHold write at :228, exactly the crash this job's own comment (:154-166) exists to repair. That row sits past the end of the 500 and is never repaired. Two days later buildSettlements claims and pays the payment out to the vendor, and the refund has nothing to come out of. getPaymentHealth's `unheldRefunds` aggregate (which has no limit) will correctly flip the page to CRITICAL, but it returns only a count — no id, no transaction — so an admin who sees `unheldRefunds: 1` has no next action.
suggested_fix: Drive the repair off the defect rather than off the whole open set: aggregate open refunds joined to transactions where `settlementHold != true` (the same shape as getPaymentHealth.js:236-250) and repair exactly those — that set is normally empty, so no limit is needed. If a limit is kept, sort by createdAt descending (newest first is where the crash-window rows are) and log when the batch fills. And have `unheldRefunds` surface the offending request ids so the count is actionable.

title: ADMIN_OVERRIDE is missing from REFUND_OPEN_STATUSES, so an approved, unpaid refund is reported to callers as closed
evidence:
constants/refund.js:57-66 lists REQUESTED, VENDOR_APPROVED, VENDOR_TIMEOUT, ADMIN_APPROVED, PROCESSING, FAILED — ADMIN_OVERRIDE (declared at :43, produced by executeRefund.js:89-90) is absent, while its sibling ADMIN_APPROVED is present.

Every presenter derives the flag from that list rather than from the stored field:
  services/refunds/executeRefund.js:403 — isOpen: REFUND_OPEN_STATUSES.includes(request.status)
  services/refunds/decideRefund.js:330 — same
  services/refunds/requestRefund.js:303 — same
  helpers/refunds/buildRefundReadPipeline.js:175 — same
while approveRefundAsAdmin (executeRefund.js:98) stores isOpen: true, and the list filter buildRefundReadPipeline.js:37 (`filter.isOpen = Boolean(query.open)`) queries the stored field. The same response can therefore say a row matched `?open=true` and carry `isOpen: false` on that row.

The model hook is derived from the same list — models/RefundRequest.js:226-228 `this.isOpen = REFUND_OPEN_STATUSES.includes(this.status)`.
failure_scenario: An admin overrides an outlet's rejection (executeRefund.js:89) and has not pressed pay yet. GET the refund: status ADMIN_OVERRIDE, statusLabel "Approved by Trydood", isOpen false. The customer app and the panel both read that as finished, so the one request that most needs chasing looks closed — and it is precisely the exception path, where a customer has already been refused once. Latent second effect: any future code that loads such a row as a document and .save()s it flips the stored isOpen to false, which drops it out of releaseSettlementHold's otherOpen guard (releaseSettlementHold.js:65-72) and out of repairMissingHolds, letting an unrelated refund's rejection release a hold sitting behind a live, approved, unpaid refund.
suggested_fix: Add REFUND_REQUEST_STATUS.ADMIN_OVERRIDE to REFUND_OPEN_STATUSES — it is an open state by every definition the file gives, and every call site that writes it already sets isOpen: true by hand (executeRefund.js:98). A migration pass over existing ADMIN_OVERRIDE rows is not needed since the stored value is already true.

title: A lost taintSettlement is never repaired, so a refund that lands inside an already-built settlement can be paid out to the vendor
evidence:
requestRefund.js:228-250 — the hold is written first, then:
  await taintSettlement({ transaction, reason: `Refund requested (${request._id})` });

Not wrapped in sendQuietly or try/catch, and not idempotently re-derivable: helpers/settlements/taintSettlement.js:38-40 keys entirely off `transaction.settlementId` captured in the caller's stale `.lean()` copy.

services/settlements/approveSettlement.js:92 — `needsRevalidation: { $ne: true }` is the ONLY gate; settlementHold is a pre-claim filter only (taintSettlement.js:12-15, helpers/settlements/index.js:42).

refundJobs.js:167-195 repairs settlementHold and nothing else — there is no re-taint sweep anywhere (grep: taintSettlement is called only from requestRefund.js:247 and handleRazorpayWebhook.js:729).
failure_scenario: buildSettlements runs at 02:00 and stamps settlementId on transaction T. At 09:00 the customer requests a refund. The RefundRequest is created and settlementHold is set, then the taintSettlement write hits a transient Mongo error (or the pod is rolled). The customer sees a 500; they tap again, hit the DUPLICATE_KEY branch at requestRefund.js:205-216, and get a 200 with reused:true — the retry never re-runs taintSettlement, because the create is what guards it. The settlement's needsRevalidation stays false and taintedTransactionIds never gets T. An admin approves at 14:00 (approveSettlement.js:92 sees nothing wrong), the NEFT goes out, and the vendor has been paid for a payment with an open refund against it. repairMissingHolds finds nothing to fix because the hold did land.
suggested_fix: Derive the taint rather than relying on one write: extend repairMissingHolds to also $addToSet/needsRevalidation any pre-payout settlement that contains a transaction with an open refund, or move taintSettlement ahead of the create so a failure aborts before the request exists.

title: With allowPartial off, floating-point on `paidAmount - alreadyRefunded` permanently blocks a customer from claiming the remainder after a vendor part-approval
failure_scenario: allowPartial is set to false. Payment ₹100.00. Customer requests the full amount; the vendor part-approves ₹69.80 and it completes, so transaction.amountRefunded = 69.80. The customer comes back for the remaining ₹30.20. Omitting `amount`: requestedAmount = round2(100 − 69.80) = 30.2, while 100 − 69.80 evaluates to 30.200000000000003, so 30.2 < 30.200000000000003 is true and they get "Partial refunds are not available. Please request the full amount." Typing 30.20 gives the same message. Typing 30.21 clears this check but calculateRefundSplit refuses it: "Only ₹30.20 of this payment can still be refunded." There is no amount the customer can submit. (Verified by evaluation; the same holds for 100.01/39.89, 100.02/89.74, 100.03/69.80 and thousands of other realistic INR pairs.)
suggested_fix: Round both sides: compare against `round2(paidAmount - alreadyRefunded)` — reuse the round2 already exported from calculateRefundSplit — and compare with the PAISA tolerance the rest of the module uses rather than a bare `<`.

title: A genuine second partial refund request is silently swallowed and answered with the first request's amount
failure_scenario: Payment ₹810, allowPartial true. The customer requests ₹300 for a missing starter — request A is created and is still awaiting the vendor. The next day, still inside the window, they discover a second problem and request ₹200 more. Everything upstream passes (their own transaction is excluded from the maxOpen count at requestRefund.js:125, the split for ₹200 computes fine), the create loses on the partial unique index, and they get 201 "Refund request raised successfully" describing a ₹300 request they already knew about. Nothing anywhere records that ₹200 was ever asked for. If the front end shows the returned amount they see ₹300; if it shows their own input they believe ₹500 is coming.
suggested_fix: Compare the existing open request against what was just asked for — same reason and same amount within PAISA — and return it as reused only then; otherwise throw a 409 that names the open request and its amount so the customer knows to withdraw it or wait.

title: applyRefundCompletion clears isOpen before it bumps amountRefunded, so a request filed in the gap is sized against a stale ceiling and can never be approved
failure_scenario: Payment ₹810 with a ₹300 refund completing. The customer is on the refund status page, sees it flip to "Refunded", and files a new request in the window between line 83 and line 137 (two DB round trips wide, and the customer is polling precisely this moment because the webhook is what changed their screen). The index is already free and amountRefunded is still 0, so requestRefund computes a ceiling of ₹810 and creates a request for the whole ₹810. The completion then writes amountRefunded=300.
