When the vendor clicks approve, approveRefundAsVendor recomputes the split against the now-correct ceiling of ₹510 and throws 422 "Only ₹510.00 of this payment can still be refunded." The vendor can never approve it — their only exit is to reject, which pushes the customer's rejection count up for a request the system generated wrongly.
suggested_fix: Write amountRefunded in the same step that closes the request, or at minimum bump the transaction total before clearing isOpen so the index is only released once the ceiling any new request will read is already correct.

title: Reminder schedule is computed from the live vendorApprovalHours setting against a deadline frozen at creation, so changing the setting mis-fires every in-flight nudge
failure_scenario: Admin raises refund.vendorApprovalHours from 24 to 48. A request created one minute ago has vendorRespondBy = +24h, so remaining = 24h and elapsedFraction = 1 - 24/48 = 0.5 >= marks[0]. On the very next hourly sweep (jobs/index.js:167-169) the vendor gets "reminder 1" minutes after the original request mail; by remaining = 12h, elapsedFraction = 0.75 and reminder 2 fires — both nudges spent by the halfway point, none in the final 12 hours when the timeout is imminent. The reverse is worse: lowering 24 to 6 gives elapsedFraction = 1 - 20/6 = -2.33 at 20 hours elapsed, so `due` is 0 and no reminder has fired at all; the first arrives only at remaining = 3h and the second at remaining = 1.5h, i.e. the vendor gets no usable warning and the request escalates to VENDOR_TIMEOUT (refundJobs.js:73-79) as a surprise — the exact outcome jobs/index.js:166 says the job exists to prevent.
suggested_fix: Derive the window from two stored fields rather than from settings: `const windowMs = new Date(request.vendorRespondBy) - new Date(request.createdAt)` (add `createdAt` to the `.select(...)` on refundJobs.js:342), then `elapsedFraction = 1 - remaining / windowMs`. That keeps the promise made to the request when it was created, which is what the doc block at lines 29-36 already argues for.

title: alreadyDecided() reports the stale pre-read status, so every vendor who loses the conditional-claim race is told the refund "has already been decided (requested)"
evidence:
services/refunds/decideRefund.js:292-303:
  /** A vendor whose click lost a race needs to know whether their colleague
   * approved it or the clock ran out — those lead to different next actions. */
  const alreadyDecided = (request) =>
    request.status === REFUND_REQUEST_STATUS.VENDOR_TIMEOUT
      ? "This refund has already gone to Trydood for review."
      : `This refund has already been decided (${String(request.status)...})`;

`request` here is the document read at line 85 / 170 by loadForBrand, never re-read. assertDecidable (lines 286-290) has already thrown unless `request.status === REQUESTED` (VENDOR_CAN_DECIDE, line 31), so at the failure sites — line 137 in approveRefundAsVendor and line 190 in rejectRefundAsVendor — `request.status` is unconditionally "REQUESTED". The VENDOR_TIMEOUT branch is dead code on the only path that reaches it. cancelRefund has the same shape at lines 255-262, where `request.status` is guaranteed to be one of CANCELLABLE.
failure_scenario: Two cases, both deterministic rather than probabilistic. (1) escalateStaleRefunds fires at the same moment an outlet manager clicks Approve: the job's conditional claim (refundJobs.js:73-79) wins and writes VENDOR_TIMEOUT; the vendor's findOneAndUpdate returns null and they are shown "This refund has already been decided (requested)." — a self-contradictory sentence, instead of "This refund has already gone to Trydood for review" which is the one that tells them to stop and hand it to the platform. (2) A brand owner and an outlet manager click Approve within the same second: the loser sees the same "(requested)" message and cannot tell whether the refund was approved or declined by their colleague — the exact distinction lines 294-296 say the message exists to draw. Same for the customer: if an admin approves at the instant they tap Withdraw, cancelRefund.js:256-261 tells them "This refund is already vendor approved and cannot be withdrawn" when it is in fact ADMIN_APPROVED.
suggested_fix: Re-read the row on the losing branch and build the message from what is actually there: `const now = await RefundRequest.findById(request._id).select("status").lean(); throwError(409, alreadyDecided(now || request));` at decideRefund.js:137, :190 and :255. Without that re-read the ternary at line 299 can never be true.

title: reverseLedgerEntry writes rows that no unique index covers, so a retried correction double-reverses
evidence:
recordLedgerEntry.js:198-218 copies only transactionId, voucherClaimId and settlementId onto the reversal — refundRequestId, payoutLegId and disputeId are dropped — and sets isReversal: true.

recordLedgerEntry.js:122-125 then computes:
  const isOncePerTransaction = !isReversal && Boolean(transactionId) && ONCE_PER_TRANSACTION_TYPES.includes(entryType);

With isReversal true the row is false there, so ledger_type_transaction_unique excludes it (partialFilterExpression requires isOncePerTransaction: true, LedgerEntry.js:179-182). With no refundRequestId it is outside ledger_type_refund_unique (LedgerEntry.js:171), and with no payoutLegId outside ledger_type_payoutleg_unique (LedgerEntry.js:162).

This is the only entry shape in the system covered by none of the three indexes. Every other writer keys into one: postCaptureEntries -> transaction index; postRefundEntries -> refund index (refundRequestId on common, line 66); postPayoutEntries and reversePayoutEntries -> payout-leg index (payoutLegId, lines 45 and 121).
failure_scenario:
An admin corrects a wrongly-posted COLLECTION and the request times out on the client, or a retry wrapper fires twice, or two admins act on the same alert. reverseLedgerEntry runs twice on the same entry. No duplicate-key error is possible, so LedgerEntry.create succeeds both times and the catch at line 150 is never entered: two opposite rows are written and the vendor is credited the amount twice. Nothing detects it — reverseLedgerEntry does not check whether a row with reversalOf === entry._id already exists, and reversalOf is enforced nowhere (it is only ever set here; no index, no validator, no query reads it).
Secondary: reversing a refund row or a payout row silently drops its refundRequestId / payoutLegId, so LedgerEntry.find({ refundRequestId }) — the shape used in __tests__/money/refundCompletion.test.js:408 and any statement scoped to a refund — returns the original but not its correction, and the refund reads as still standing.
suggested_fix: Before creating, look for an existing row with reversalOf === entry._id and return it as duplicate: true. Additionally give reversals a key the indexes can see — e.g. carry refundRequestId/payoutLegId through and add a denormalised isReversal boolean to the two partial filters so { refundRequestId, entryType, isReversal } is unique — otherwise the append-only correction mechanism has no idempotency at all.

title: GST-inclusive capture credits the convenience fee gross of tax and credits the tax again
failure_scenario:
Set tax.isGstEnabled true and tax.isGstInclusive true (both admin-settable, validator/settings.js:109, models/Setting.js:259). Slab fee 10, 18% -> gstAmount 1.53, taxOnTop 0; the customer pays exactly 10.00 of fee.
Ledger credits: PLATFORM_REVENUE +10.00 and TAX_PAYABLE +1.53 = 11.53 credited against 10.00 of cash actually received. getPlatformTotals reports 10.00 of revenue that is really 8.47 net of a tax liability the same ledger has already booked separately — the 1.53 is counted on both sides of the platform's books. The exclusive branch is correct (fee 10 + taxOnTop 1.53 = 11.53 charged, 11.53 credited), so the defect is specific to the inclusive toggle and will appear the day it is switched on, silently, as a 1.53-per-claim overstatement of margin.
suggested_fix: Post CONVENIENCE_FEE net of embedded tax: amount should be round2(pricing.convenienceFee - (pricing.isGstInclusive ? pricing.gstAmount : 0)). The exclusive path is unaffected because gstAmount there is already outside convenienceFee. The same net figure must then be used for split.convenienceFeeRefund's ledger row.

title: getPlatformTotals has no index for its query shape and rescans every platform row ever written
failure_scenario: The admin dashboard asks for last month's platform totals. Mongo can use the single-field { account } index, but it must then fetch and filter every PLATFORM_REVENUE, PLATFORM_COST and TAX_PAYABLE document ever written to test occurredAt. postCaptureEntries writes up to four of those per claim (CONVENIENCE_FEE, PLATFORM_PROMO_COST, GATEWAY_FEE, TAX_COLLECTED), and the collection is append-only by design (models/LedgerEntry.js:17-26 — rows are never deleted, isDeleted is never set). At 10k claims/month that is ~40k docs examined in month one and ~480k by month twelve to return a single month, growing without bound and with no .limit() to cap it. The cost of the month-of-March report rises every month forever.
suggested_fix: Add ledgerEntrySchema.index({ account: 1, occurredAt: -1 }) so the range is served by the index rather than by a post-filter, and drop the now-redundant field-level index:true on account.

title: The sparse {settlementId:1} index cannot serve the settlementId:null eligibility query it was created for, so every hourly build full-scans Transaction once per brand
failure_scenario: With a million voucher-claim transactions, buildSettlements runs hourly (jobs/index.js:188). brandsWithEligibleMoney (buildSettlements.js:124-134) issues a distinct over `settlementId: null` and claimTransactions issues an updateMany over the same predicate once per active brand (settlementClaims.js:113). None of these can use the index that was added for them; the best available is `{purpose:1, status:1, createdAt:-1}` (Transaction.js:456), which does not narrow on settlementId at all. Every unclaimed row — the overwhelming majority of the collection — is examined on every build for every brand, so the job's cost grows linearly with lifetime volume and with brand count simultaneously. Released rows are the only ones in the index, because releaseSettlementClaims writes an explicit `$set: { settlementId: null }` (settlementClaims.js:163), which makes the index's contents look plausible while the hot query still scans.
suggested_fix: Drop `sparse` and give settlementId an explicit `default: null` so the unclaimed rows are indexed, then make it a compound partial index matching the real predicate — e.g. `{ settlementId: 1, brandId: 1, fundsReceivedAt: 1 }` partial on `{ purpose: VOUCHER_CLAIM, settlementHold: false }`. Register it in assertMoneyIndexes so a missing one is reported at boot.

title: releaseStaleClaimHolds has no limit and makes one Razorpay call per row, so a backlog turns a 15-minute sweep into an unbounded run
failure_scenario: Razorpay is unreachable for two hours during a busy evening. Every PENDING claim past quoteTtlMinutes takes the catch branch at claimJobs.js:88, counts as keptForCapture, and stays PENDING — so the backlog only grows. The 15-minute tick then loads the entire backlog into memory and issues one gateway call per claim, serially. The run outlives the 15-minute JOB_LOCK_LEASE_MINUTES (constants/job.js:30) if enough heartbeats are missed, at which point another instance acquires the lock and starts the same serial gateway walk alongside it; jobLock.js:107-111 only warns and lets the first run continue. The job still returns `{checked: N, cancelled: 0, keptForCapture: N}` and is recorded as a success in JobLock (jobLock.js:147-151), so the health page shows the sweep as healthy while no slot has been released for hours.
suggested_fix: Add `.sort({ createdAt: 1 }).limit(200)` to match every other sweep, and return a `lookupFailures` count so a run where the gateway was unreachable for every row is distinguishable in JobLock.lastResult from a run where there was nothing to do.

title: One brand's error aborts the entire nightly build - every remaining brand is skipped, and the failing brand's already-claimed rows are stranded
failure_scenario: 800 brands are eligible. On brand #180, a transient MongoNetworkError hits the Settlement.updateOne at line 188 - after claimTransactions has already stamped settlementId on brand #180's rows. The throw propagates out of buildForBrand, out of the for loop, and out of buildSettlements. Brand #180 is left as a DRAFT holding rows with netPayable 0, which is the permanently-stranded state above; brands #181-800 get no settlement at all this tick, and the log says only `buildSettlements failed: <message>` with no count. On the next tick brands #181-800 recover (eligibility has no periodStart floor), but brand #180 never does.
suggested_fix: Wrap the buildForBrand call in a per-brand try/catch that logs brandId and pushes to a `failed[]` array returned in the job result, so one brand cannot cost the run. Pair it with a compensating release: on a throw after the claim, call releaseSettlementClaims(settlement._id) and void the idempotencyKey (`STL:VOID:<_id>`) so the period is rebuildable, rather than leaving a DRAFT holding rows.

title: settlementNumber is never generated - the admin search filter always returns nothing and every vendor notification prints a dash
failure_scenario: A vendor emails support quoting a payout. Support opens the settlements list and searches by settlement number; buildSettlementListFilter sets filter.settlementNumber = "TD/STL/26-27/000123" and the query matches zero documents (every stored settlementNumber is undefined), so support concludes the settlement does not exist. Every vendor payout email and stuck/overdue/ledger-drift admin alert renders the identifier as "-", so an admin receiving five overdue alerts cannot tell which settlement each concerns without opening the DB by _id.
suggested_fix: Generate the number through the existing Counter pattern (helpers/vouchers/generateUniueCode.js is the template: findOneAndUpdate with $inc and upsert, retrying on DUPLICATE_KEY against the settlement_number_unique partial index) at the DRAFT -> PENDING_APPROVAL transition - not at shell creation, so an abandoned draft does not burn a number of record. Until then, drop the settlementNumber search filter rather than leaving a filter that silently never matches.

title: A configured `delayDays: 0` is silently rewritten to 3, building the wrong period
evidence:
services/settlements/buildSettlements.js:62
  const delayDays = Number(settings.delayDays) || 3;

0 is falsy, so a legitimately configured 0 becomes 3. The value is accepted everywhere upstream:
  models/Setting.js:399  delayDays: { type: Number, default: SETTLEMENT_DEFAULTS.delayDays, min: 0 },
  validator/settings.js:162  delayDays: Joi.number().integer().min(0).max(30).optional(),
and helpers/settings/assertSettlementTimingRule.js:39-46 permits 0 whenever the refund windows sum to 0.

The neighbouring lines get this right - buildSettlements.js:63-64 use `Number(x) || 0`, where 0 is the intended fallback - so the bug is specific to the one setting where 0 is meaningful.

delayDays feeds both canonical boundaries (buildSettlements.js:72-73) and therefore the idempotencyKey at :144.
failure_scenario: An admin configures same-day settlement for a pilot: settlement.delayDays = 0, refund.windowHours = 0, vendorApprovalHours = 0, adminBufferHours = 0. assertSettlementTimingRule passes (0 >= 0). Setting.js stores 0. getCustomerConfig.js:112 returns 0 (it uses `??`, correctly). buildSettlements.js:62 turns it into 3. Every build then targets periodEnd = end of IST day T-3 instead of T, so nothing captured in the last three days is ever settled on the promised schedule, and the idempotencyKey names the wrong day. Nothing errors, and the settlements that appear look correct for T-3.
suggested_fix: Use the nullish coalescing the rest of the config layer uses: `const delayDays = Number(settings.delayDays ?? SETTLEMENT_DEFAULTS.delayDays);` - getCustomerConfig has already applied the default at helpers/settings/getCustomerConfig.js:112, so the `|| 3` fallback here is redundant as well as wrong.
